extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and readers interested in crime fiction/noir and craft of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical distinctions for writing and evaluating hardboiled and noir fiction, with practical advice on point of view, voice, thematic focus (taboo/desire), and how genre labeling and cultural context shape reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardboiled vs. Noir (moral clarity vs pervasive fallenness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled is distinct from noir: hardboiled extends the pioneer/Western hero into the city where the hero (detective/cop) is somewhat fallen but at story's end has usually done the right thing and order is to an extent restored. Noir is different: 'in noir, everyone is fallen, and right and wrong are not clearly defined and maybe not even attainable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when situating a story: hardboiled tends toward restorative endings and a heroic figure who re-establishes some order (example: Law and Order formula), while noir accepts pervasive moral ambiguity and a lack of clear resolution. Consider which ethical architecture you want your narrative to inhabit before plotting or choosing perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noir's historical resonance (thrives in social instability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir has historically thrived after large social upheavals (e.g., 1940s after Depression and WWII; 1970s with Watergate and Vietnam) because it speaks to eras when certainties are shaken and people sympathize with characters who distrust or operate outside governing systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for contemporary resonance, align noir themes with moments of social/ political anxiety—readers respond when the genre reflects their sense that structures of authority 'don't make sense any longer.' Use historical analogies (Depression/WWII, Watergate) to inform atmosphere and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noir as a space for taboo and forbidden desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir has always depicted taboos—sexual and otherwise—where desires 'run amok' (examples given: incest, adultery, same-sex desire when it was considered a perversion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want the emotional/visceral charge associated with noir, consider exploring repressed, forbidden, or socially proscribed desires and the moral complexity they create. Treat taboo material as thematic fuel rather than gratuitous shock; noir often uses taboo to expose social anxieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of the 'tough guy' and masculinity in crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled 'tough guy' tropes conceal a recurring 'gender panic': unlike hypermasculine Hollywood versions (Humphrey Bogart), many hardboiled novels show masculinity as insecure—Marlowe risks emasculation and lacks control unlike Spillane's Superman-like Mike Hammer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing male protagonists or pastiches, be attentive to subtler characterizations: vulnerability, fear, and a crisis of identity can produce richer, truer hardboiled characters than simple macho posturing. Be wary of letting filmic archetypes erase the genre's textual ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre labels and marketing language can diminish nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels like 'domestic,' 'domestic noir,' 'psychological thriller,' 'beach read,' or 'chick lit' are shorthand but can carry gendered or diminishing connotations—in Abbott's words she 'bristle[s]' at 'domestic' because it's laden with stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics should be cautious using reductive labels; consider how a descriptor will frame reader expectations and might strip complexity from work. Use labels strategically for marketing, but resist letting them dictate critical reading or creative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view selection should serve suspense and information control
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of POV is crucial to suspense: inhabiting the dark/mysterious character's head can eliminate mystery ('If the reader knew everything about Diane... there would be no opportunity for suspense'). Alternating POVs is tricky because you must 'play fair' with readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a POV that preserves the necessary unknowns. Use a 'proxy' or less-informed narrator to tell a story involving a mysterious character, or anchor the narrative in someone who doesn't fully understand other characters. If using multiple POVs, carefully manage what each knows and when to reveal it to maintain suspense without cheating the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative fairness when using interior perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: When you're 'in a character's head, you have to—to a degree—surrender that character's knowledge to the reader.' This imposes fairness obligations on sleight-of-hand and information control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whose knowledge the reader has access to and avoid concealed omniscience. If you want to mislead or withhold, choose techniques (unreliable narrator, omission, selective focalization) that are consistent with the chosen POV and ethical toward the reader's expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor the novel with a stable presence (protagonist as grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often you want to ground the novel with a stable presence, an anchor; the protagonist can serve this role even if they are imperfect or not likable (example: Kit in Give Me Your Hand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an anchored perspective to orient readers emotionally and structurally. The anchor needn't be morally exemplary—it's a reference point whose steadiness helps sustain narrative momentum and reader investment amid moral ambiguity or psychic turmoil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding authentic voice for unfamiliar perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can inhabit characters from worlds they've not lived in (Abbott struggled with and then found the cheerleader narrator in Dare Me); the act of 'finding her voice' changed the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume inability to write outside your experience—focus on voice discovery through immersion, empathy, and craft. Voice authenticity matters more than identity matching; readers respond when the narrator's voice feels true and specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural moment and market dynamics affect genre popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success (e.g., Gone Girl, The Girl on the Train) made publishers more willing to take chances on certain female-centered crime novels; sociopolitical events (2016 campaign, #MeToo, Weinstein scandal) also surface themes that make such books resonate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing and cultural context when writing or marketing work: topical currents can amplify interest in certain themes or voices. That said, long-term quality remains decisive—'the book stands if the book stands.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Author identity, pseudonyms, and ethical/mercenary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some male authors adopt female or androgynous pseudonyms to sell novels; Abbott notes she doesn't 'begrudge' it but recognizes it can feel mercenary—ultimately she insists 'the book stands if the book stands.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the ethical optics of pseudonym use, especially when identity is central to the book's themes. While market tactics may be understandable, consider how concealment might affect reader trust or critical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember that film adaptations often simplify literary ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: When hardboiled novels reached Hollywood, much of their ambiguity and subversive take on identity were erased in favor of cool, unambiguous screen heroes (e.g., Bogart versions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you're influenced by film noir, revisit the literary sources to capture their moral and psychological complexity rather than relying on cinematic shorthand. Resist modeling prose or character complexity solely on film tropes that flatten nuance.
